hints: Look at N right at the top edge in Fig. 3.2 - this is the lining facing the air in the lumen, with a dark fringed border on top.
walkthrough:
Locate N On The Lumen Edge**
N is the thin dark layer forming the innermost lining of the trachea. In the trachea this lining traps dust and microbes in mucus and then sweeps it upwards.

Link Fringed Border To Function**
The fringed top edge is made of cilia beating in coordination. That identifies the tissue as ciliated epithelium, often pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium in the airways.

hints: Look at O just below the lining - small rounded clusters of cells with pale central spaces, typical of secretory tissue.
walkthrough:
Spot The Glandular Clusters**
O points to many small circular profiles in the connective tissue under the epithelium. Each has a ring of cells around a central lumen, the classic appearance of a gland in section.

Link To Trachea Function**
The trachea needs a constant supply of mucus to trap pathogens and dust for the cilia to move. Those submucosal secretory clusters are the mucous glands.

hints: Look at P - the large pale band with many small dark nuclei scattered in lacunae, sitting outside the glands and next to smooth muscle.
walkthrough:
Recognise The Cartilage Appearance**
P is a broad, light-staining plate with chondrocytes sitting in small spaces. That matrix plus scattered cells is characteristic of cartilage.

Link To Fig. 3.1 Plan**
In Fig. 3.1 the dotted C-shaped ring keeps the trachea open. Fig. 3.2 is a magnified view of one end of that ring, so P must be the cartilage that supports the airway and prevents collapse.

hints: Think about what smooth muscle does to the diameter of the airway when it contracts versus when it relaxes.
Link a wider airway during vigorous exercise to oxygen need at the alveoli - what happens to resistance to airflow and gas exchange?
walkthrough:
From Relaxation To Wider Lumen**
Smooth muscle in the wall squeezes the airway narrower when it contracts. When it relaxes the elastic wall recoils outward, so the trachea and bronchi dilate and the lumen diameter increases.

From Wider Airway To More Oxygen**
A wider tube gives much less resistance to airflow, so ventilation increases for the same breathing effort. More fresh air reaches the alveoli per minute, increasing oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide removal to satisfy the higher respiration rate in exercising muscle.
Final answer: trachea/bronchi widen, reducing resistance to airflow; more air/oxygen reaches alveoli for greater gas exchange to meet increased oxygen demand.

hints: Compare number of polypeptides - elastin is described as a single polypeptide, so recall how many chains make up one collagen molecule.
Compare regularity - elastin has glycine at irregular intervals forming random coils, so recall the regular glycine pattern and coiled shape of collagen.
walkthrough:
Single Chain Versus Three Chains**
Elastin here is one single polypeptide. Collagen is larger and more ordered - three polypeptide chains wound together, giving it quaternary structure. That three-stranded arrangement is key to its high tensile strength.

Random Coil Versus Regular Triple Helix**
In elastin glycine is abundant but at irregular intervals and the chain forms stretchy random coils. In collagen glycine is at every third position, allowing the three chains to pack tightly into a regular triple helix. Pick any two of these contrasts for the two marks.

Final answer: collagen has three polypeptides / quaternary structure whereas elastin has one; glycine occurs every third residue in collagen whereas irregular in elastin; collagen forms a triple helix whereas elastin forms random coils.
